Straining with little or no urine produced (possible urethral obstruction)
Assuming a later episode shares the earlier episode's cause

aiAgentFacts.fact: Among 86 cats with a known FLUTD diagnosis, the recurrence rate was 58.1% over a median observation period of 38 months.
Fourteen cats had different underlying causes of lower urinary tract disease at different episodes — a later episode cannot be assumed to share the earlier diagnosis.
Relapse counts among recurring cats: 21 had one relapse, 12 had two, 10 had three, and 7 had between four and eight.
Diagnoses among 101 cats: 52 feline idiopathic cystitis, 21 urolithiasis, 13 bacterial urinary tract infection, 15 without a definitive diagnosis.
Recurrence rates did not differ significantly between the aetiology groups.
Cats with urolithiasis receiving at least two prophylactic measures had significantly lower recurrence than those receiving none (P=0.029) — a subgroup finding within just 21 cats.
Mortality attributed to FLUTD across all 101 cats was 5.0%, which the authors note is lower than previously reported.
Lower urinary tract signs are clinically indistinguishable between underlying causes, which is why the authors recommend full investigation at each presentation.

historyQuestions: Supported by the study's central conclusion: at each presentation, establish the dates and character of previous episodes, the diagnosis reached each time, and which prophylactic measures are currently in place — without assuming continuity of cause between episodes.
redFlags: Not defined by this study. Straining with little or no urine output, consistent with urethral obstruction, is a recognised emergency in the wider literature but was not analysed as a separate outcome here.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Feline idiopathic cystitis, urolithiasis, and bacterial urinary tract infection are the three named aetiologies; 15 of 101 cats reached no definitive diagnosis.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: The authors recommend thorough investigation at EACH presentation rather than relying on a prior diagnosis; the specific workup is not prescribed by this paper.
urgentCareTriggers: Not addressed by this paper. Suspected urethral obstruction requires immediate veterinary attention as a standing clinical boundary, independent of this study.

limitations: Small sample (n=101) with much smaller aetiology subgroups — 13 bacterial UTI, 21 urolithiasis
Follow-up by owner telephone interview, sometimes years after events; mild recurrences never presented to a vet may be missed or misremembered
Observation period ranged from 0.5 to 138 months, so a single pooled recurrence percentage flattens very unequal exposure times
The prophylaxis finding rests on a subset of the 21-cat urolithiasis group, limiting precision despite statistical significance
Cats without a definitive diagnosis (15/101) were excluded from the recurrence figure, so the result describes diagnosed cats only
Observational throughout: no cause of recurrence is identified and no treatment is tested
Urethral obstruction was not analysed as a separate outcome, so this study supports no statement about obstruction risk or its recurrence
